nameStory: This oceanic wanderer is named after Charles B. Cory, an American ornithologist who made significant contributions to bird science in the late 1800s. Cory was particularly known for his work on seabirds, making it fitting that this graceful ocean glider bears his name as it cuts through Atlantic swells.
description: Cory's Shearwater is a large seabird that spends most of its life gliding effortlessly over ocean waves. These impressive birds are about the size of a small gull, with long, narrow wings perfectly designed for riding wind currents without much flapping. They have grayish-brown upperparts and clean white underparts, giving them a two-toned appearance when seen from below. During most of the year, they roam widely across the Atlantic Ocean, only coming to land to breed on remote islands.

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Watch for their distinctive 'shearing' flight - long glides on stiff wings that barely flap, banking side to side as they follow the contours of ocean swells with remarkable grace

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than most gulls with a robust, barrel-shaped body and exceptionally long, narrow wings that span about 3-4 feet from tip to tip

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Brownish-gray above and bright white below, creating a clean contrast that's especially visible when the bird banks during flight

idTips.label: Bill Shape
idTips.description: Thick, hooked yellow bill that looks almost chunky compared to gull bills, designed for grabbing fish and squid from the ocean surface

idTips.label: Head Pattern
idTips.description: Pale grayish head that blends smoothly into the white throat and breast, without the sharp contrasts seen in many gulls

idTips.label: Ocean Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen following fishing boats or feeding in flocks over schools of fish, rarely coming close to shore except during storms

habitat: In New England waters, look for Cory's Shearwaters far offshore in deep ocean waters, typically many miles from land. They prefer areas where warm and cold ocean currents meet, creating rich feeding opportunities over the continental shelf and beyond. You're most likely to spot them from whale-watching boats, ferries to offshore islands, or during pelagic birding trips that venture into deep Atlantic waters.

seasonality.spring: Begin arriving in New England waters in late spring as they follow warming ocean currents and abundant fish populations northward from their wintering areas.
seasonality.summer: Most commonly seen during summer months when they're actively feeding in productive New England waters, often visible from whale-watching boats and pelagic birding trips.
seasonality.fall: Peak numbers occur in early fall as birds gather before beginning their southward migration, sometimes driven closer to shore by storms.
seasonality.winter: Largely absent from New England waters as most birds move to warmer southern Atlantic waters for the winter months.

funFact: These ocean athletes can lock their wings in place using a special tendon system, allowing them to glide for hours without a single wingbeat - essentially 'surfing' the invisible waves of air that bounce off ocean swells, making them one of the most energy-efficient fliers in the bird world.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Greater Shearwater, but Cory's lacks the dark cap and white collar that Greater Shearwater shows. Remember: Cory's has a 'clean' head that gradually transitions from gray to white, while Greater Shearwater looks like it's wearing a dark cap with a white collar.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'shearwater' comes from their flight style - these birds literally appear to 'shear' through the water's surface as they glide just inches above the waves. Until recently, Cory's Shearwater was considered the same species as Scopoli's Shearwater from the Mediterranean, but scientists now recognize them as separate species.
compareHints: Cory's Shearwater is much larger and paler than its closest relative, Scopoli's Shearwater, which is found in the Mediterranean. While both share the same graceful flight style and general body plan, Cory's has a more robust build and lighter overall coloration. In New England waters, you're only likely to encounter Cory's Shearwater, as Scopoli's rarely ventures into the western Atlantic.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Cory's Shearwater, Scopoli's typically shows more contrasting dark wing edges and a more distinct dark patch on the bill tip.
